One of the most common risks with the successful business is simple. How large can it get before it saturates
the market? This is a key question for investors who may have counted on many more years of growth
in order for the company to generate enough earnings to rationalize a higher valuation.
The problem typically stems more from lofty investor expectations rather than
the company misunderstanding the market potential. But, of course, either can happen.
Take Home Depot, for example. In January 2000, which was fiscal 99, they had 930 stores. However,
they were targeting over 1900 stores by January 2004. This is a more than doubling of the
store base in four years. For the fiscal year ending ending 1999, they generated 38 billion in
revenues and opened 160 new stores. Rather than asking the question
immediately, whether 1900 stores is too many, a conservative investor could start by inverting the problem.
Instead of starting with the question, with the risk of not achieving 1900 stores, start with
with the return of what you'd get if they did. While this may seem contradictory to Warren
Buffett's, quote, two rules of investing. Rule number one, don't lose money,

and a margin of safety are mathematically the same thing. So when gauging the potential return, we are

adequate return. This is the equivalent of building a margin of safety.
